There is a particular kind of quiet that exists only in the hour before dawn, when the world hasn't yet decided what kind of day it will be. The streetlights are still on, but they look tired, as if they know their job is almost over. Birds start tentatively, one or two at first, testing the air before the chorus arrives.

I find myself drawn to these in-between moments. We spend so much of our lives oriented toward destinations, the next meeting, the weekend, the moment when things finally settle. But the transitions are where things actually happen. A kettle is never more alive than the seconds before it whistles. Bread rises in the dark of the oven light. Ideas often arrive not at the desk but in the shower, on a walk, in the gap between one thought and the next.

Maybe that's why I like old train stations and public libraries. They are built for waiting. Nobody goes to a library to be finished. People sit with half-formed questions and let them grow. A stranger two tables away is reading about beekeeping, and you will never know why, and that unanswered curiosity feels like a small gift.

I also think about how little we notice of ordinary things. The way cold water changes the texture of a cup. The smell of cut grass that lingers after the mower has gone. The fact that every face you pass is carrying a whole private weather system you'll never see.

Paying attention is not dramatic. It doesn't make headlines or earn anyone a promotion. But it might be the closest thing we have to a practice of gratitude, a way of saying yes to what's already here before rushing toward whatever comes next.

The birds are louder now. The light has turned the color of weak tea. The day has decided to begin, and somehow I'm not quite ready for it, which may be the most honest feeling I have all morning.
